newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan activists taking islands protest to Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan activists taking islands protest to Tokyo.

text.p: Taiwanese activists on Wednesday pledged to demonstrate at Japan's foreign ministry in Tokyo to protest a landing by Japanese rightists on an East China Sea island claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan.

The announcement came a day after organisers called off plans to sail on Sunday to the disputed archipelago, known to Chinese as the Diaoyus and Japanese as the Senkakus. They cited a shortage of funds and pressure from Taiwan's government.
"We have temporarily called off Sunday's sea protest action. Instead, we will travel to Tokyo and protest outside Japan's foreign ministry," organiser Ching Chia-shou said.
He said ethnic Chinese activists from Taiwan, Hong Kong and the United States would join the Tokyo protest on May 17 or 18.
The activists had planned to sail on Taiwanese fishing boats to the islands on May 18 and attempt a landing to reassert Taiwan's claim of sovereignty.
The longstanding row over the islands flared again after right-wing Japanese lawmaker Shingo Nishimura and supporters landed on one of the uninhabited islands on May 6 and raised Japan's flag.

Ching said his anti-Japanese protest was intended to remind Japan of its history of brutal militarist expansion, including its 1937-1945 occupation of China and atrocities committed by Japanese troops in the Chinese city of Nanjing.
"We will hold placards and posters showing Japanese slaughtering thousands of Chinese people in Nanjing," he said.
Ching condemned Taiwan's cabinet-level Council of Agriculture for warning Taiwanese fishermen and fishing companies against leasing boats to the activists.
"Because of the warning, we were unable to lease the boats to go to the Diaoyu islands," he said, branding Taiwan's government as "gutless" and "afraid to offend Japan".
He said the activists would stage a landing once they had raised funds and secured boats for their mission.
Ching called on Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui to speak out against Japan at his annual news conference on Thursday.

The 1996 erection of a lighthouse on one of the islands by a Japanese rightist group lit nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan and sparked a wave of landing attempts, one of which left a Hong Kong activist dead.

In October, Taiwan and Hong Kong activists broke through a Japanese maritime cordon, went ashore on one of the islands and hoisted the flags of China and Taiwan in a bid to assert Chinese sovereignty over the rocky outcrops.
